assumptions_made.assumption: High-value customers (power users) are the primary driver of the retention drop and should be the focus
assumptions_made.explanation: Data confirms power users represent 52% of revenue with 78% retention. However, the candidate didn't validate whether the 13-point drop is concentrated in this segment or spread across all cohorts.

assumptions_made.assumption: Operational/service issues (returns, shipping, inventory) are the root cause of churn for high-value customers
assumptions_made.explanation: Support data shows delivery delays (28%), returns (24%), and quality issues (18%) are top complaints. Delivery time (4.2 days vs 2.8 competitor avg) and on-time rate (82% vs 92% benchmark) support this. However, this is inferred rather than directly validated.

assumptions_made.assumption: Cost-cutting without diagnosis would worsen retention
assumptions_made.explanation: Valid concern given the data shows service quality issues are already problematic. However, the candidate didn't explore which costs could be cut without impacting service.

assumptions_made.assumption: A loyalty program change may have triggered the drop
assumptions_made.explanation: The candidate raised this as a hypothesis but no data was provided to validate or refute it. This remains speculative.

summary: The candidate demonstrated strong diagnostic instincts by correctly identifying power users as the priority segment and linking operational pain points (delivery, returns) to churn. However, the analysis was incomplete and lacked rigor—the candidate made intuitive leaps without validating whether the retention drop is actually concentrated in high-value segments, failed to explore the 14-30 day post-purchase churn window, ignored critical product category insights (48% repeat in Home & Living vs 15% in Electronics), and did not develop a specific action plan with measurable diagnostics. The recommendation to focus on high-value segment retention is directionally correct but insufficiently supported by data-driven prioritization or competitive benchmarking.
